points.title: The problem
points.lead: A parent who needs a nurse waits hours in a clinic queue, and the clinic is short of staff.

facts.text: Most households rely on public clinics, where the average wait is over three hours.
facts.source: Stats SA General Household Survey 2025; Ritshidze 2023

facts.text: Families care for older parents at home with no planned nursing in between clinic trips.

points.answer: The problem is access. Most South African households depend on public clinics, the average clinic wait is over three hours, and clinics are short of staff. Families caring for a parent at home have no planned nursing in between those trips.

points.title: How big it is
points.lead: Two in three households use a public clinic, and most people have no medical aid.

points.answer: 66.8% of households, 13.4 million, normally use a public clinic. The average wait is 3 hours 7 minutes, 75% of clinic managers say they are short of staff, and only 15.5% of people have medical aid. Public clinics see about 128.3 million primary-care visits a year. Sources: Stats SA General Household Survey 2025 and Ritshidze 2023.

points.title: The solution, and what makes it different
points.lead: Planned nurse visits at home and a shorter clinic queue, on one health record, with GilbertOne as the assistant inside.

facts.text: MyThuso Home: a registered nurse visits the home, and a named clinician reviews where needed.
MyThuso Clinic: booking, digital queueing and reminders for public clinics.
GilbertOne answers in South Africa's 11 official languages from our own server in South Africa.
Emergency words are caught on the phone itself, before any AI model, and sent to 10177 or 112.
A nurse confirms every case that is not green before it becomes a booking.

points.answer: MyThuso brings planned nurse visits into the home and shortens the clinic queue, on one health record. I am GilbertOne, the assistant inside it. I answer in South Africa's 11 official languages from a server in South Africa, I catch emergencies before any AI model sees the message, and a nurse confirms every case that matters. Others in the market each cover one lane, such as home nursing, virtual advice or private bookings. MyThuso joins home care and the public clinic on one record.

points.title: Socio-economic importance
points.lead: Care closer to home, less travel for families, and paid work for registered nurses.

facts.text: of every R299 planned visit goes to the nurse
facts.source: MyThuso funder brief, October 2026: illustrative economics

facts.text: Fewer clinic trips for older and chronically ill patients, and less time off work for the family members who take them.
Booking and queueing for public clinics is priced below a half-time clerical post: R4,000 a month per clinic.
Nurse jobs created in the pilot.

points.answer: MyThuso brings care closer to home, so older and chronically ill patients make fewer clinic trips and family members lose less time from work. It creates paid work for registered nurses: in our planning figures, R224 of every R299 visit goes to the nurse. For clinics, booking and queueing is priced at R4,000 a month, below a half-time clerical post. These are planning figures, not results.

points.title: Stage of the technology
points.lead: The technology proof of concept is done. Next is a clinical pilot, then scale.

facts.text: Live on web, iPhone and Android since 21 September 2026, for orientation and notes.
Our own model runs on a server in South Africa and passed 54 of 54 safety tests.
About technology readiness level 6: a working prototype shown in a realistic setting.
Booking, payments, nurse dispatch and SOS are simulated in the demo.

The first pilot starts in Gugulethu, Cape Town, where the founder grew up, then grows to three areas: 30, then 90, then 180 users, with 6 nurses, 2 doctors, 3 leased branded cars and about 1,080 home visits over 18 months. Every user gets a branded, tracked device.
facts.source: MyThuso TIA proposal and summary decks, 28 October 2026

facts.text: Before real patients: a data protection impact assessment, an Information Officer and data kept in South Africa.

points.answer: The technology proof of concept is done. MyThuso has been live on web, iPhone and Android since 21 September 2026, and our own model runs on a server in South Africa, where it passed 54 of 54 safety tests. We estimate technology readiness level 6. Booking, payments and dispatch are still simulated. The next step is a clinical pilot in Gugulethu, Cape Town, after the privacy paperwork is signed, and then scale.

points.title: The ask
points.lead: R12.5m over 18 months for a pilot that starts in Gugulethu and grows to 180 users, released in three gates against evidence.

facts.text: pilot budget over 18 months, first site Gugulethu, Cape Town
months 1 to 5: entity and IP baseline, devices tested, a costed team trained. Gate: acceptance evidence before any patient.
facts.source: MyThuso TIA proposal and summary decks, 28 October 2026

facts.text: months 6 to 12: paid duties start and users grow to about 90 across two areas, with 4 nurses and 2 doctors. Gate: acceptance evidence on visits, incidents and costs.
facts.source: MyThuso TIA proposal and summary decks, 28 October 2026

facts.text: months 13 to 18: 180 users in three areas, delivered under independent evaluation, and contracts for the next cohort. Gate: the evaluation's evidence before scale.
facts.source: MyThuso TIA proposal and summary decks, 28 October 2026

points.answer: We ask for R12.5 million for an 18-month pilot that starts in Gugulethu, Cape Town, and grows to 180 users in three areas, with six nurses, two doctors, three leased branded cars and about 1,080 home visits. Every user gets a branded, tracked device, and KTC gets fewer routine trips, not more work. It is released in three tranches of R3.5 million, R5 million and R4 million, and each tranche unlocks only against acceptance evidence.
